citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $U$ be a connected oriented smooth handlebody with connected boundary $\Sigma$ of genus $h$, and let $m=h+k-1>0$ disjoint proper compression disks cut it into $k$ actual smooth balls. Write $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_m$ for their boundary circles. Let $\beta$ be a finite disjoint union of smooth circles transverse to the $\gamma_i$.

There is an orientation-compatible Riemann surface structure $j$ on the actual $\Sigma$ such that each component of its surface cut along the $\gamma_i$ is conformally an explicit Riemann sphere with finitely many pairwise disjoint round disk interiors removed. This conformal identification is smooth up to every boundary circle. Each $\gamma$–$\beta$ crossing has a $j$-holomorphic coordinate in which those two arcs are precisely the real and imaginary lines. The finitely many crossing charts can have disjoint closures.

Consequently every transverse product-torus generator in $\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ has an actual standard product-integrable chart with $T_\gamma=\mathbb R^m$ and $T_\beta=i\mathbb R^m$ locally. In particular a specified generator has a standard complex chart flattening $T_\gamma$ without changing the standard symmetric-product structure there.

This is an auxiliary complex-model construction for the full balanced disk count geometry. It asserts no antiholomorphic involution, additional real ovals, disk emptiness, boundary index or count, transversality or invariance.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U\subset S^3$ be a compact smooth three-manifold with smooth boundary and let a finite disjoint family of smooth rank-two embedded disks be proper in the following broad sense: each disk has its boundary in $\partial U$ and its interior in $\operatorname{Int}U$. No transversality at its boundary is required. Suppose the topological cut components are three-balls. Then the disks can be replaced by arbitrarily $C^1$-close neat compression disks with exactly the SAME boundary curves, unchanged outside arbitrarily small boundary collars. The new topological cut components correspond to the old ones. After ordinary finite smooth corner rounding the new components are smoothly parametrized standard balls, with labelled disk faces and compatible product collars. Reattaching the disk neighborhoods recovers the actual $U$ and the new disks as their cocores.

The replacement can be supported away from any fixed compact set disjoint from the disk boundary collars, in particular the actual knot arcs and any supplied simultaneous bridge witnesses disjoint from the disks. These objects, their endpoints, ordered pairing and face avoidance are retained. Only the auxiliary compression witnesses change; the surface, attaching curves and actual knot stay fixed. The transport across the initial tangency is a boundary-fixing homeomorphism, smooth separately off its tangency edges; a smooth ambient boundary-preserving diffeomorphism changing tangency is not claimed. The smooth standard-ball assertion uses the full smooth three-dimensional Schoenflies theorem under Countable Choice, rather than a general topological smoothing theorem.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U$ be a connected oriented smooth handlebody with boundary $\Sigma$. Supply $m$ pairwise disjoint smooth compression disks NEAT at their boundary, actual compatible disk-face collars, and compatible roundings of the cut corners. Suppose cutting along them gives $k\ge1$ parametrized smooth balls. Put $h=m-k+1$, and suppose $h\ge0$.

These finite data construct an orientation-compatible finite polygon presentation of the ACTUAL surface $\Sigma$, with word $\prod_{i=1}^h A_iB_iA_i^{-1}B_i^{-1}$ when $h>0$, and the standard finite sphere presentation when $h=0$. The construction gives the quotient map and finite subdivision into smooth face pieces, rather than inferring their existence from an abstract surface classification. In particular these are the actual finite polygon data required by the diagonal-degree and multipointed sphere-index suppliers.

The construction allows all pairs of faces of the cut balls, including loop pairs on the same ball. It does not require any knot arcs and does not change $\Sigma$ or its orientation. Neat disks, parametrized cut balls and their compatible face collars are hypotheses: no auxiliary tangential disk normalization or identification of a raw cusp cut with a smooth corner is asserted here.

Assume countable choice. Fix integers $m\ge2$, $b\ge1$, $p\ge0$, and positive integers $d_1,\ldots,d_b$ with $\sum_i d_i=m$. There is a compact connected smooth oriented surface $S$ with exactly $b$ boundary components and a positive branched covering
$$\pi:S\longrightarrow\overline{\mathbb D}$$
of degree $m$, unramified near its boundary, such that its boundary components have covering degrees $d_1,\ldots,d_b$. It has exactly
$$N=m+b-2+2p$$
distinct simple interior branch values, each with one ramified preimage of local form $w\mapsto w^2$. Its Euler characteristic is
$$\chi(S)=m-N=2-2p-b.$$
The construction specifies actual charts and a complex structure making the interior map holomorphic. It is a finite slit-gluing construction from a factorization into transpositions; no existence theorem for Riemann surfaces or generic-map selection is assumed.

For degree one a connected positive branched disk cover from a compact surface has no ramification and is a disk mapped diffeomorphically onto the target. Thus positive degree-one covers cannot realize the values $2-2p-b$ above with $b=1,p>0$. This result constructs a surface and covering; it does not identify an arbitrary supplied surface with that surface, realize a given Whitney class, or supply an incidence map into a symmetric product.

Assume Countable Choice. The following explicitly constructed compact oriented smooth surfaces admit finite smooth triangle data, with any specified finite set of boundary points as vertices:

1. A finite disjoint union of smoothly parametrized planar closed disk-with-holes regions, glued in finitely many pairs of boundary circles by specified smooth circle diffeomorphisms and compatible signed product collars, whenever the resulting surface is oriented. One may leave some circles unglued. A round sphere with finitely many round disk interiors removed is included by placing a stereographic pole in one removed disk.
2. A surface obtained from the first construction by deleting finitely many additional smoothly parametrized disks with closures inside the planar-piece interiors and gluing in specified smoothly parametrized annuli along some of their boundary circles, with compatible product collars. Before this operation one may separate finitely many closed subcollars of the original seams as explicit annular pieces.
3. The actual compact positive branched disk covers supplied by the finite-transposition construction, including the degree-one disk case.

Here finite smooth triangle data means finitely many face-to-face embedded triangular disks, each parametrized from a Euclidean closed triangle by a smooth map with nonsingular derivative in a surface chart on a neighborhood of that triangle. Interior vertex links are circles and boundary links are intervals. Parametrizations of the two occurrences of a common edge may differ by an increasing smooth interval map; the image cellulation has a compatible finite abstract simplicial model after finite subdivision. These are precisely the supplied smooth face and incidence data needed by the finite tangent-field index and finite smooth surface matching arguments.

No triangulation or smoothing result for an arbitrary topological surface or an arbitrary prescribed tangential graph is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $S_0,S_1$ be compact connected oriented smooth surfaces with nonempty smooth boundary. Supply finite smooth triangle presentations: face-to-face triangular disks, with circular interior vertex links and interval boundary links, whose parametrizations are smooth nonsingular maps in surface charts through each closed triangle. Suppose the two presentations have the same Euler characteristic and the same positive number $b$ of boundary components.

For any bijection of their boundary components, any orientation-preserving smooth circle maps on the paired components, and any prescribed inward collar germs, there is an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $B:S_0\to S_1$ realizing those circle maps and their collar identifications. In particular one may prescribe one marked point on each boundary circle. The diffeomorphism can additionally agree with finitely many prescribed orientation-preserving interior diffeomorphism germs at distinct points with distinct target points, while retaining the boundary collars.

All surface presentations are supplied finite data. No triangulation-existence, arbitrary topological smoothing, three-dimensional smoothing or unproved smooth classification result is assumed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed Riemann surface and $m\ge1$. Give $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ its usual complex charts of elementary symmetric coordinates in disjoint support disks. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to X$ be the quotient and $p_i:\Sigma^m\to\Sigma$ its factor projections. For $i<j$ let $\Delta_{ij}=\{z_i=z_j\}$, and put $R=\sum_{i<j}\Delta_{ij}$, with coefficient one on every pair diagonal, including at their intersections. Then there is a holomorphic line-bundle isomorphism
$$q^*\det_{\mathbb C}(TX)\cong\left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^m p_i^*T\Sigma\right)\otimes\mathcal O(R).$$
Under this isomorphism the holomorphic section $\det(dq)$ of
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}\left(\bigotimes_i p_i^*T\Sigma,q^*\det_{\mathbb C}(TX)\right)$$
corresponds to the canonical divisor section of $\mathcal O(R)$. In particular its zero divisor is exactly $R$, even at tuples with three or more equal entries; no transverse-intersection or simple-branch hypothesis is needed for the bundle identity.

Here $\mathcal O(R)$ is constructed by the actual local defining functions in the proof. For a smooth map $F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m):C\to\Sigma^m$ from a closed oriented surface with supplied finite smooth triangle data, the identity implies the degree formula
$$\deg\bigl((qF)^*\det(TX)\bigr)=\sum_i\deg(f_i^*T\Sigma)+\sum_{i<j}\deg\bigl((f_i,f_j)^*\mathcal O(\Delta)\bigr),$$
where $\Delta\subset\Sigma\times\Sigma$ is the ordinary diagonal. Degree means the finite face-winding degree of a complex line bundle. Whenever a pulled-back diagonal section has finitely many isolated zeros, its degree is the sum of their signed local winding indices; at a transverse coincidence this is the sign of $d(f_i-f_j)$ in an oriented surface coordinate. Degrees remain defined if two maps coincide identically.

For $m=1$ the empty divisor has its trivial line and constant section one; $q$ is the identity. For $m=0$ all determinants and tensor products over the one-point symmetric product are trivial and the degree formula is zero. This result does not identify the diagonal class in surface cohomology, compute a sphere's degree, prove a Maslov/domain formula, or realize arbitrary Whitney classes by incidence covers.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $K\subseteq M$ be compact, and let $W\subseteq M$ be open with $K\subseteq W$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:M\to [0,1]$ that equals $1$ on an open neighbourhood of $K$ and satisfies $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq W$.

Let $S$ be a compact oriented smooth surface with smooth boundary and a supplied finite smooth triangulation. This means finite face-to-face triangular disks with circular interior vertex links and interval boundary vertex links; each face has an orientation-preserving parametrization by a closed Euclidean triangle whose derivative is nonsingular and smooth on a neighborhood of that triangle in a surface chart. Let $v$ be a supplied smooth tangent field on $S$, with finitely many isolated interior zeros, none on the triangulation's vertices or edges. Suppose $v$ is a positive multiple of the positively oriented tangent along every boundary component. The boundary may be empty.

At each zero $p$, define $\operatorname{ind}_p(v)$ as the winding of the nonzero coordinate vector $v$ along a sufficiently small positively oriented coordinate circle around $p$. This integer is independent of the positively oriented coordinate and of the small circle. Then, with $V,E,F$ the given finite triangulation counts,
$$\sum_{p:v(p)=0}\operatorname{ind}_p(v)=V-E+F=\chi(S).$$
There is no choice assumption. The assertion is conditional on the supplied smooth triangulation and field; it does not claim a triangulation or generic field exists in a more general category.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed connected Riemann surface, $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ with its standard complex structure, and $m\ge1$. For $a\in\Sigma$ put $E_a=\{a\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$. This is a smooth complex hypersurface, including at repeated tuples. The universal incidence hypersurface $\mathcal E=\{(a,D):D\in E_a\}\subset\Sigma\times X$ carries a smooth complex divisor line bundle with its canonical section, whose zero set is $\mathcal E$ with multiplicity one.

For a smooth map $v:S\to X$, where $S$ is an oriented sphere or a closed disk, define $n_a(v)$ as the degree of the pullback point-divisor line bundle; for a disk use the canonical section to trivialize it on the boundary, and require $v(\partial S)\cap E_a=\varnothing$. The proof constructs this integer by elementary frame winding. It is defined even when a sphere lies wholly in $E_a$.

For a sphere, $n_a(v)$ is independent of $a$ on all of $\Sigma$. For a disk whose boundary tuples have all entries in a finite union of curves $\Gamma\subset\Sigma$, it is independent of $a$ on each connected component of $\Sigma\setminus\Gamma$. If $v^{-1}(E_a)$ is finite and the map is holomorphic on a neighborhood of every one of these points, then
$$n_a(v)=\sum_{z\in v^{-1}(E_a)}\operatorname{ord}_z(F_a\circ v)\ge0,$$
where $F_a$ is any local holomorphic defining function of the smooth hypersurface $E_a$. Each term is a positive integer. Thus the degree agrees with proper holomorphic intersection multiplicity, while divisor containment is handled by its degree definition and actual point movement rather than an unsupported proper-intersection assumption.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented Riemann surface with an actual finite oriented polygon as in the sphere-index theorem, $m\ge1$, and put $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$. Let $\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta$ be two disjoint-within-system smooth curve families of size $m$, transverse to each other, with product tori $L_\alpha,L_\beta$. Give two smooth fixed-end Whitney disk models $u,v$ from the same generator $x$ to the same generator $y$, constant near their two marked boundary corners, with their actual fixed product end data. Use the auxiliary complex-structure homotopies and actual relative-index realizations specified in the relative Whitney index theorem. Domain coefficients mean the integer relative degrees of the point-divisor lines, not a holomorphic representative assumption.

For any such pair, $D(u)-D(v)$ has boundary a sum of full attaching circles. The coefficient on each oriented circle is the angular winding difference of the corresponding labelled boundary paths, with their source-boundary signs. In particular, if $D(u)=D(v)$ as region chains, their boundary paths on each labelled alpha circle are homotopic relative their endpoints, and likewise on each labelled beta circle. After these boundary homotopies the difference of their smooth relative classes is represented by a sphere $A$ with $n_z(A)=0$. Consequently
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}(u)=\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}(v),$$
before source translation, on all the stated higher Sobolev and allowed smooth weighted realizations. Thus actual Fredholm index is well defined on the set of REALIZED Whitney domains, including classes with positive, zero or negative marked multiplicities. No assertion that every integer region chain is realized is made.

The analogous statement holds for two smooth disks based at the same point of a single product torus $L_\gamma$, with equal one-system domains: their boundary loops are based homotopic, and their boundary Maslov indices and compact-disk Fredholm indices agree. Their fixed-node indices also agree whenever that bounded point-trace realization is used. The finite polygon hypothesis is supplied for the original embedded balanced $S^3$ data by the broad-input application in the sphere-index theorem. No full formula $e(D)+n_x(D)+n_y(D)$, normalized relative or absolute grading, invariance, or arbitrary-domain representativity is included.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented genus-$h$ Riemann surface with a supplied orientation-compatible finite polygon presentation as in the finite diagonal-degree theorem, and let $m\ge1$. Put $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$. For every smooth sphere map $u:S^2\to X$ and every $z\in\Sigma$, define $n_z(u)$ to be the degree of $u^*\mathcal O(E_z)$, where $E_z=\{z\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$ and degree is finite face winding, including when the sphere image is contained in $E_z$. Then
$$\deg(u^*\det_{\mathbb C}TX)=(m+1-h)n_z(u).$$
In particular this formula is valid for arbitrary smooth sphere classes, not only holomorphic maps or simple incidence curves. It is unchanged on replacing the standard complex tangent bundle by a homotopic complex structure on the same real tangent bundle.

Let a smooth fixed-end Whitney strip model with actual product end frames represent a class $\phi$, and let $\phi\#u$ be its interior connected sum with such a sphere, using a specified attaching path and keeping the physical boundary and end data fixed. Its actual real Fredholm indices, before source translation, satisfy
$$\mu(\phi\#u)-\mu(\phi)=2(m+1-h)n_z(u).$$
Thus when $m=h+k-1$ the sphere shift is exactly $2k\,n_z(u)$. This includes all positive and negative sphere degrees. In particular the finite polygon can be constructed, rather than separately supplied, when $\Sigma$ bounds a smooth handlebody embedded in $S^3$ with $m=h+k-1$ smooth proper rank-two compression disks cutting it topologically into $k$ balls. This application permits tangential disk boundaries: auxiliary disk replacement and smooth cut-ball reconstruction are proved prerequisites below. No full domain/corner formula for a nonspherical Whitney class, boundary-degeneration count, absolute grading or invariance theorem is included.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E\to\overline{\mathbb D}$ be a smooth complex vector bundle of rank $m\ge1$, with complex multiplication $J$, and let $F\subset E|_{\partial\mathbb D}$ be a smooth oriented totally real real subbundle of rank $m$. Let $P$ be a smooth real-linear first-order operator on sections with exact Cauchy–Riemann symbol: for real smooth $h$ and smooth $\xi$,
$$P(h\xi)=hP\xi+h_x\xi+h_yJ\xi.$$
Use smooth positive definite metrics and finite smooth charts to define $H^r(E)$ by weak derivatives for integers $r\ge1$. Let $X_0$ be the $H^1$ closure of smooth sections with boundary values in $F$, and put $X_q=H^{q+1}(E)\cap X_0$, $Y_q=H^q(E)$ for integers $q\ge0$. Only the zeroth boundary condition is imposed.

There is a smooth global complex frame of $E$ and an integer $k$ in which the boundary condition is
$$F(e^{it})=e^{ikt}\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb R^{m-1}$$
and the actual operator is $\partial_x+i\partial_y+B$ with smooth real-linear zeroth-order coefficient $B$. Equivalently, before this reduction, if $C(t)$ is the complex matrix whose columns are any smooth periodic oriented real frame of $F$ in any global complex frame, then
$$k=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{(\det C)'(t)}{\det C(t)}\,dt.$$
Such frames exist, and this integer is independent of both choices.

Every actual realization $P_q:X_q\to Y_q$ is bounded Fredholm with real index $m+2k$. Its kernel is the same set as the $H^1$ kernel, its range is $Y_q\cap\operatorname{Ran}P_0$, and inclusion in $L^2$ identifies its real cokernel with that of $P_0$. For $\xi\in X_0$ and $P\xi=f\in H^q$,
$$\|\xi\|_{H^{q+1}}\le C_q(\|f\|_{H^q}+\|\xi\|_{H^1}).$$
The inverse of $P_0$ from its $H^1$ kernel complement to its closed range is bounded, and its restriction gives a bounded range inverse $H^q\cap\operatorname{Ran}P_0\to X_q$. The statement applies to an actual geometric linearization along a smooth disk with oriented totally real boundary. It does not assert its surjectivity, compute a Heegaard domain formula, or supply a puncture or gluing theorem.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented smooth surface with positive area form $\eta$ and an orientation-compatible complex structure $j$. Use its smooth complex symmetric product $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m\Sigma$, $m\ge1$, and the descended product symplectic form $\omega$ off the diagonal. Let $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m$ be disjoint embedded circles, and likewise $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m$, with every alpha-beta intersection transverse. Let $T_\alpha,T_\beta\subset X$ be their product tori. Fix finitely many points $p$ of $\Sigma$ away from all these circles and the associated divisors $E_p=\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}\Sigma$.

The intersection $K=T_\alpha\cap T_\beta$ is finite and disjoint from the diagonal and all $E_p$. There exist pairwise disjoint neighborhoods $U_x$ of its points, with closures disjoint from those protected sets, and smooth coordinate charts $q_x$ centered at $x$ taking $T_\alpha,T_\beta$ to $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$. There is a smooth almost complex structure $J_*$ on $X$ equal to $\operatorname{Sym}^m(j)$ near the diagonal and all $E_p$, taming $\omega$ elsewhere, and exactly $i$ in each $q_x$ chart near $x$.

More generally any smooth family $J_t$ with the first two properties can be modified inside the $U_x$, retaining its values outside them and near all protected sets, to have those exact product-integrable values on smaller neighborhoods for every $t$. The constant path $J_*$ therefore provides a genuine admissible geometric choice with the local hypotheses needed for product-integrable end asymptotics. No regularity or moduli count is asserted for that path.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed connected Riemann surface with positive area form $\eta$, and let $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$, $m\ge1$, with standard complex structure $J_0$, quotient $q:\Sigma^m\to X$, and repeated-point locus $\Delta$. Off $\Delta$, the product form $\Omega=\sum_l\operatorname{pr}_l^*\eta$ descends to $\omega$. Fix a smooth target metric $g$ and finitely many attaching curves with finitely many complementary regions $R$. A product torus $L_\gamma$ uses one point on each of a labeled system of $m$ pairwise disjoint curves $\gamma_i$ among those curves. Choose a point $a_R$ in each region. Suppose a smooth path $J_t$ agrees with $J_0$ on a fixed neighborhood $V$ of $\Delta$ and on a fixed neighborhood of every $E_{a_R}=\{a_R\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}\Sigma$, and tames $\omega$ on $X\setminus V$.

Let $u$ be a smooth $J_\tau$-holomorphic map for any fixed $\tau\in[0,1]$, either from the oriented sphere, or from a compact disk with its entire boundary on $L_\gamma$. Let $n_R(u)=n_{a_R}(u)$ be the actual absolute or relative divisor degree constructed by the point-divisor intersection lemma. Then every $n_R(u)$ is a nonnegative integer, and a constant $C$ depending only on the fixed geometry and path satisfies
$$E_g(u)\le C\sum_R n_R(u)\int_R\eta.$$
This includes spheres lying entirely in $\Delta$ or in a point divisor; no off-diagonal-end hypothesis is present.

For a sphere all region coefficients equal one nonnegative integer $d_0$, and $n_a(u)=d_0$ for every $a\in\Sigma$. For a one-torus disk, let $A_i$ be the connected components of $\Sigma\setminus\bigcup_j\gamma_j$. Its coefficient function is constant on each $A_i$, say $b_i\ge0$, and its domain is $\sum_i b_i[A_i]$; in particular its boundary has only $\gamma$ curves. If one marked point $z_i$ is chosen in each $A_i$ away from all attaching curves, then $n_{z_i}(u)=b_i$.

Consequently a sphere with one zero point-divisor degree is constant. A one-torus disk with all the degrees $n_{z_i}$ zero is constant. The disk conclusion uses one marked point in each actual complement component, as provided by a complete marked cut system, and does not require any admissibility assertion about two-torus periodic domains or a Maslov-index formula. Applying them to a zero-mark degeneration still requires a proved additivity statement for the divisor degrees of its limiting components.

derivations.claim: First obtain the geometric polygon data required by [F4]. Transport an abstract handlebody to a standard ball with finitely many one-handles embedded in $S^3$, by the finite handlebody parametrization construction in [F1]. Apply its broad same-boundary neat preparation there, retaining every attaching circle, and select the finitely many actual smooth cut-ball parametrizations it supplies. The neat-cut polygon construction of [F1] then gives an actual oriented finite polygon, which transports back to the original surface. Its chosen target complex structure $j$ is never replaced. These same cut-ball data give the smooth planar component parametrizations used below. Suppose now $k\ge2$ and fix $A=A_i$. The ball-cut parametrizations in [F1] make its compact cut closure a planar surface. Let $e$ be the number of attaching circles with just one boundary copy on this component and $\ell$ the number with both copies on it. Its boundary count is $e+2\ell$ and $$\chi(A)=2-e-2\ell.$$ Here $e\ge1$: the finite graph with the cut components as vertices and each attaching circle as an edge is connected, since regluing it recovers the connected $\Sigma$. A vertex with no edge to another vertex would be isolated, impossible when there are at least two vertices. Glue the two boundary copies of each internal circle using the actual signed collars. The result $S_0$ is the actual embedded subsurface obtained by filling those internal circles in $\Sigma$, with $e$ external boundary circles, Euler characteristic still $\chi(A)$ and an orientation-preserving inclusion into $\Sigma$. These assertions follow by the collar gluing: a circle has Euler characteristic zero, so identifying a pair changes no finite cell count. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

Put $a=0$ if $e\ge2$ or $\ell=0$, and put $a=1$ otherwise. If $a=0$ take $S=S_0$ and let $f$ be its inclusion. If $a=1$, choose a tiny proper closed arc $I$ of one internal circle, with $x_j$ in its interior. A positive smooth surface chart $H$ straightens this arc to $[-2c,2c]\subset\mathbb R$, with $x_j=H(0)$. It need not be holomorphic for the given $j$. Replace the interior of a small ellipse around this interval by the parametrized annulus $1\le|\zeta|\le R$, $R>1$, with map $$f(\zeta)=H(c(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})).$$ On its outer circle this is a diffeomorphism onto that ellipse boundary; use its univalent outer collar as the gluing collar to the unchanged remainder of $S_0$. Thus $S$ is a smooth compact surface, $f$ is smooth, and its interior maps diffeomorphically onto $\operatorname{Int}S_0\setminus I$. The inner circle maps to the two banks of $I$, with two quadratic tips, smooth even at those tips. Its label is that internal $\gamma_j$; choose either of the two inverse points of $x_j$ on it as its marked boundary point. Each external boundary circle has its unique marked point over its generator coordinate. The resulting surface has $$r=e+a\quad\hbox{boundary circles},\qquad \chi(S)=2-e-2\ell-a.$$ It has finite smooth triangle data by [F2]: separate the internal seam collar as an annular piece before deleting the ellipse, then use its planar gluing and annulus-insertion clauses. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

If $r=1$, the choice in step 2.1 forces $e=1,\ell=0$, so take the identity disk cover. Otherwise [F2] supplies an actual positive branched cover $p:F\to\overline{\mathbb D}$ of degree $r$, with exactly $r$ boundary components of degree one and $$N=2r-2+2\ell\quad\hbox{simple ramification points},\qquad\chi(F)=2-2\ell-r=\chi(S).$$ Its branch values are distinct. Choose for each ramification point a distinct target point of $\operatorname{Int}S$, avoiding the finitely many inverse images under $f$ of all inactive generator coordinates. Since $f$ is an orientation-preserving local diffeomorphism on the interior, prescribe at this point an orientation-preserving germ $B$ such that $f\circ B$ is complex linear in the ramification coordinate of $F$ and a $j$-holomorphic target coordinate. This is the explicit smooth germ $f^{-1}$ composed with that linear coordinate map. By [F2] extend these finitely many germs to an actual oriented diffeomorphism $B:F\to S$, with every boundary component paired to its label and its unique point over $p=1$ sent to the selected point over $x_j$. This supplies the required smooth matching; a topological surface homeomorphism alone would not suffice. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

For $z\in\overline{\mathbb D}$ take the unordered fiber values of $f\circ B$ over $p^{-1}(z)$ and adjoin the remaining $m-r$ generator coordinates as constants. This defines a smooth map $u_A$ to $X$. Away from ramification the root functions are smooth sheet inverses. Near a ramification point their two active values are holomorphic functions of the two square roots of $z-q$, by the exact prescribed germs in step 3.1; their elementary symmetric functions are therefore smooth there. All other roots have regular sheet coordinates there, and no branch value has two ramification points. This proves smoothness at every repeated-root tuple, even though the whole map is not asserted holomorphic. On the physical boundary each active labelled circle contributes exactly one root, because its $p$ boundary degree is one. The other labels have their distinct fixed generator roots. Thus $u_A(\partial\mathbb D)\subset L$ and $u_A(1)=x$. The interior root map $f\circ B$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism onto $\operatorname{Int}S_0$ with the possible slit removed. Every generic point of $A$ has exactly one inverse root, and every point off the attaching system outside $A$ has none. Its relative divisor degrees are consequently exactly the unit chain $A$. [F2, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Choose a smooth field $V$ on $\Sigma$, tangent and nonzero on every $\gamma_j$, and nonzero at all the finitely many ramification image values. Extend its prescribed circle collars by finite bumps and apply [F3] on their compact complement, also prescribing nonzero values at those finitely many additional points. Apply the same finite parameter transversality on the finitely many supplied triangle edges and vertices: their dimensions are less than the field rank two, so a transverse zero set there is empty. Thus it has finitely many isolated zeros away from the circle system, ramification images and triangle one-skeleton. Their indices inside $A$ sum to $\chi(A)$ by [F3], with every hypothesis of its facewise index calculation met. To meet the positive-boundary convention of that supplier, on the CUT planar component multiply $V$ by $e^{i\theta}$, with $\theta=0$ or $\pi$ on each boundary collar according to its orientation. Extend this scalar by finite collar bumps. This introduces no zero or index change, so the sum for the original global field is still $\chi(A)$, even at the two opposite copies of an internal circle. Pulling its zeros back by $f\circ B$ preserves their indices and gives exactly one inverse point for each. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Off root collisions take the square of the wedge of $dq(V)$ in the $m$ roots, a section $\sigma$ of $(u_A^*\det TX)^2$. Its squared Vandermonde expression in [F3] extends continuously by zero at collisions. Every pulled-back field zero contributes twice its field index. Every simple ramification contributes one positive zero: the two exchanged roots are local holomorphic coordinates there by step 3.1.
